title: No blaming
hookLine: let no one hear you blame court life, not even yourself (Meditations 8.9)
carry: turn back to what you can do

cards: Listen to any break room, any family group chat, any line at the post office. This place is a mess. My boss doesn't get it.
The traffic in this city. My job is killing me. Complaining can be friendly; it's how strangers bond in a stalled elevator.
And it can quietly take over a whole life. Marcus Aurelius had an emperor's share of things to complain about. In book eight he wrote himself a rule about it, in a single sentence.

teach.b: Meditations eight, nine, says: let no one hear you any longer finding fault with life at court, or with your own life. That's all.
Remember Marcus's stepmother picture from book six: the court as the stepmother, philosophy as the mother. The court was where the flattery was, the scheming, the endless petitions.
He had every reason to grumble, and he tells himself to stop, at least out loud.

teach.h: NOT WITH YOUR OWN LIFE EITHER.
teach.b: Then the second half: or with your own life. Complaints about the world are one habit; complaints about yourself are another. I'm hopeless.
I always mess this up. Marcus closes both. Not because things are perfect, but because complaining, in either direction, doesn't change the next action, and it trains the mind to see only the faults.
This isn't a ban on naming real problems. The rule is about finding fault, not about fixing things.

teach.h: A PLAN IS NOT A COMPLAINT.
teach.b: A plan to fix something isn't a complaint. Telling a friend you're struggling isn't either.
The target is the background hum of blame, the grumbling that goes nowhere. Listen for it for one day, and it can be startling how much ordinary talk it fills.
Marcus's rule is simple: catch it, and stop, even mid-sentence. Then turn back to what you can actually do.

how: Readers of Marcus sometimes keep a no-complaining rule, catching grumbles about their circumstances or themselves and turning them into a plan or letting them go.

o: Marcus's rule: no grumbling about his life, or court life
a rule against ever naming a real problem aloud
a promise never to judge other people's choices

s: let no one hear you find fault with court life, or with your own.
Marcus says never to name a real problem
the rule is about finding fault; a plan to fix something isn't a complaint.
the rule covers complaining about yourself too
he adds 'or with your own life.'

games.q: you're halfway through your usual complaint about work. by 8.9, what do you do?
o: stop mid-sentence, and turn to what you can do.
games.why: Meditations 8.9: let no one hear you any longer finding fault with court life or with your own.

practice: Bring to mind your most familiar complaint, about work, a person, the city, yourself, and hear it in your own voice; then let it stop halfway and notice the quiet after it.
In that quiet, ask whether there's one thing you can actually do about it. If there is, picture it; if there isn't, just breathe.

wordCard.voice: No blaming. Marcus's one-line rule: let no one hear you find fault with your circumstances, or with your own life. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: turn back to what you can do. A plan isn't a complaint, and neither is asking for help. Day five hundred ninety-eight, complete.
